1A.title: Questions and answers
words: Too interested in other people’s private lives
A person who applies for a job
A document with your education and work history
The money you earn from your job
A question that asks for more details
A feeling you can’t explain; intuition
Making you feel shy or stupid
Cannot fail; very easy to use
A person who loves computers or technology
Time for your job vs time for your life
The person who asks the questions
Wanting to know or learn things

g.title: Question formation
g.rule:
Good questions follow a few fixed patterns.

auxiliary before the subjectHow long have you worked here? · Why didn't she call?
subject questions: no do / didWho told you? · What happened?
preposition at the endWhat are you thinking about? · Who did you go with?
indirect questions: normal word orderCould you tell me where the office is? · Do you know if he has left?

ex.q: Could you tell me what time ___?
Who ___ this report?
What are you waiting ___?

talk: Interview your partner for a job they would love. Ask at least six questions.
What is the strangest question you have ever been asked?

r.text:
Most applicants prepare for the obvious questions. They know why they want the job, and they can describe their strengths without blinking. What they are rarely ready for is the question that seems to have nothing to do with work.

One recruiter in Almaty always asks candidates what they had for breakfast. "I'm not being nosy," she explains. "I want to know whether they can make small talk with a stranger. Half our work is conversation."

Another asks how many windows there are in the city. Nobody knows the answer, and that is the point. He is interested in how a person thinks aloud, and in which follow-up questions they ask.

Do such questions work? Research suggests that a gut feeling formed in the first minute is hard to change. A foolproof method does not exist. Could you tell me what you had for breakfast?

ex.q: What does the Almaty recruiter ask about?
Why does she ask it?
o: To check whether candidates can make small talk

ex.q: The windows question has a correct answer that candidates should know.
What does research suggest?
o: First impressions are hard to change

l.intro: Two friends compare job interviews.

script.t: Manneh, how did the interview go? Who interviewed you?
The head of the department. She asked me what I would do if I were an animal.
Seriously? What did you answer?
I said a dolphin. Then she wanted to know why I had left my last job.
That's a fair question. Did she ask about salary?
No, but she asked how I felt about my work–life balance, which seemed a bit nosy.
Do you know whether you got it?
Not yet. My gut feeling is good, though. The small talk at the end went well.
Could you tell me who else applied?
Forty applicants, apparently. I sent a follow-up email this morning.

ex.q: Who interviewed Manneh?
Which question did he find nosy?
Manneh already knows that he got the job.
What did he do this morning?

1B.title: It’s a mystery
words: A person who says they can see the future
Two similar things happen by chance at the same time
Information that helps solve a mystery
An idea that tries to explain something
Nice to your face, nasty behind your back
A person who reads your future in cards or palms

g.title: Auxiliary verbs; the…, the… + comparatives
g.rule:
Auxiliaries do a lot of work in conversation.

short answers and echo questionsI've seen a ghost. — Have you?
So / Neither + auxiliarySo do I. · Neither have I.
emphasisI do believe you. · She did call, I promise.
the + comparative, the + comparativeThe more I read about it, the less I understand.

ex.q: You believe in coincidences, ___?
The longer I waited, ___ I became.
I didn't see anything strange. — Neither ___ I.

talk: Describe something that happened to you which you can't explain.
Do you believe some people can predict the future? Why or why not?

r.text:
When my aunt moved into her flat, the neighbours told her that the previous owner, a retired pianist, had died there. My aunt does not believe in ghosts, and neither do I. Nevertheless, something strange did happen.

Every night at about eleven she heard three notes on a piano. She does not own one. The neighbours don't either. She checked the radio, the television and her phone. The longer she listened, the more nervous she became.

A sceptical friend offered a theory: old pipes can sound musical. A plumber came. The pipes were fine, he said, and so was the heating.

The mystery was solved by a child. The boy upstairs had been given a toy keyboard, and his bedtime was eleven. "I do like a rational explanation," my aunt says. "Although the more I think about it, the less I understand why he always played the same three notes."

ex.q: Who had lived in the flat before?
What did the aunt hear every night?
The plumber found a problem with the pipes.
What was the real cause?
o: A boy with a toy keyboard

l.intro: A sceptic and a believer discuss a strange evening.

script.t: Rosa, you don't really believe that psychic, do you?
I do, actually. She knew my grandmother's name.
Did she? You probably mentioned it yourself.
I didn't. And she said I'd get a phone call, and I did, an hour later.
That's a coincidence. The more people she sees, the more often she's right.
You're so sceptical. Have you never had a spooky experience?
I have, actually. But there's always a theory that explains it.
So do I have no evidence?
None. And the longer you talk to her, the more clues you give her.
Well, I'm not superstitious, but I'm going back next week.

ex.q: What did the psychic know?
Daniyar thinks the phone call was a coincidence.
According to Daniyar, why is the psychic often right?
o: She sees a lot of people

ex.q: What is Rosa going to do?

lessons.title: Reading: The flat on the third floor

2A.title: Doctor, doctor!
words: A sign that you are ill
To hurt a joint by twisting it
Someone who always thinks they are ill
A painful bubble on your skin from shoes
To lose consciousness for a short time
A long piece of cloth to wrap an injury
Your body reacts badly to something

g.title: Present perfect simple and continuous
g.rule:
Both link the past to now; the choice depends on your focus.

result, a completed action, how manyI've seen the doctor twice this month.
activity, how long, a recent activity with a visible resultI've been feeling dizzy all week. · You've been running.
non-action verbs → simpleI've had this cough for ages.

ex.q: How long ___ these tablets?
I ___ three appointments this week.
She ___ (know) her doctor since she was a child.

talk: Have you or someone you know ever had an accident or an injury? What happened?
What have you been doing recently to stay healthy?

r.text:
Ten years ago, when people felt unwell, they waited to see whether it would pass. Now they reach for their phone. Doctors say that more and more patients have already diagnosed themselves before they walk into the surgery.

Dr Sadykova has been working as a GP for twenty years. "I've seen a real change," she says. "This morning a man came in who had been reading about rare diseases all night. He had a headache and a rash, and he was convinced it was something terrible. It was an allergy to washing powder."

She is not against online information. Patients who have been following good advice often recover faster. The problem is that the internet has never examined anyone.

Her rule is simple. If you have had a symptom for more than a week, or if it has been getting worse, make an appointment. "And please," she adds, "don't tell me what the forum said."

ex.q: How long has Dr Sadykova been a GP?
What was wrong with the man?
The doctor is completely against online information.
When should you make an appointment?
o: If a symptom lasts more than a week or gets worse

l.intro: A customer asks a pharmacist for advice.

script.t: Good morning. How can I help?
I've been feeling dizzy since Monday, and I've got a rash on my arm.
Have you taken anything for it?
I've taken two painkillers a day, but they haven't helped.
Have you been eating anything unusual?
Now you mention it, I've been trying a new diet. And I've had food poisoning twice this year.
I think you should have a check-up. Have you seen your doctor?
Not yet. My wife says I'm a hypochondriac. I've already been to the surgery four times this month.
Even so, a rash and dizziness together need a proper look.
All right. I've been putting it off for too long.

ex.q: How long has the customer been feeling dizzy?
The painkillers have helped.
What does the pharmacist recommend?
What does his wife call him?

2B.title: Act your age
words: Differences between young and old people
Not working any more because of age
Someone the same age as you
Wear smart clothes for a special event

g.title: Using adjectives as nouns; adjective order
g.rule:
Two things to know about adjectives.

the + adjective = a group of peoplethe young · the elderly · the unemployed (plural verb)
nationalitiesthe French · the Japanese; but the Italians, the Kazakhs
order: opinion → size → age → colour → origin → materiala lovely long black Italian leather coat

ex.q: ___ often have more free time than people who work.
She was wearing a ___ dress.
The young ___ (be) more worried about climate change.

talk: Should people dress their age? Describe what you think suits different generations.
Describe the clothes of someone whose style you admire.

r.text:
Fashion has always had opinions about age. The young, we are told, can wear anything, while the middle-aged should choose something sensible, and the elderly should disappear into beige.

Not everyone agrees. In Seoul there is a group of retired men, all over seventy, who are photographed every weekend in beautiful tailored grey wool suits and bright leather shoes. They have become more famous than most models.

Meanwhile, the rules for the young are changing too. A scruffy old cotton hoodie used to be the uniform of the teenager. Today some of the smartest dressers at university are the students.

Designers have noticed. One brand now uses models aged from sixteen to eighty in the same campaign. "The old are our best customers," its director says. "They have the money, the time, and, frankly, the taste."

Perhaps the only real rule is this: wear what fits, and wear it as if you chose it.

ex.q: What are the elderly traditionally told to wear?
Who has become famous in Seoul?
The brand uses only young models.
What does the director say about older customers?
o: They have money, time and taste

l.intro: A mother and her daughter argue about clothes.

script.t: Arman, you're not going to the interview in that scruffy hoodie, are you?
It's a nice grey cotton hoodie, Mum. The young don't wear suits any more.
The middle-aged do. And the interviewer is fifty.
That's the generation gap. You think trendy means untidy.
I think a smart dark blue jacket never looks old-fashioned.
The rich can afford jackets like that.
There's a lovely old Italian wool one in your father's wardrobe.
Dad's? It's enormous. And striped.
Try it. The retired know a few things about first impressions.
Fine. But I'm keeping my denim shirt.

ex.q: What does Arman want to wear?
What does his mother suggest?
Arman thinks young people still wear suits.
What will Arman keep?

lessons.title: Using adjectives as nouns; adjective order

g.title: Narrative tenses, past perfect continuous; so / such…that
g.rule:
A good story uses four past forms.

main eventsWe boarded and the plane took off.
background in progressPeople were sleeping when the turbulence began.
earlier action · earlier activity in progressThe pilot had warned us. · We had been flying for six hours.
so + adjective · such + (a) nounIt was so frightening that I couldn't speak. · It was such a long flight that I read two books.

ex.q: We ___ for an hour when the announcement was made.
It was ___ bad weather that the airport closed.
When I got to the gate, the flight ___ (already / leave).

talk: Tell the story of your best or worst journey by air, train or bus.
Are you a nervous traveller? What helps you?

r.text:
I had been travelling for nineteen hours when I boarded the last flight home. I had a boarding pass for seat 14A, by the window, and all I wanted was to sleep.

Somebody was already sitting there. He was about eighty, and he was looking at the clouds as if he had never seen any before. His daughter explained that he had not flown since 1975, and that he had been waiting for this day for months. Would I mind the aisle seat?

I did mind. I was so tired that I could hardly speak. But I took 14C.

The turbulence started over the mountains. It was such a rough descent that several passengers were praying. The old man was laughing. He had been a pilot, his daughter told me, and he had landed in worse.

When we disembarked, he shook my hand. I had not slept at all, and it was the best flight I had had in years.

ex.q: How long had the writer been travelling?
Who was sitting in seat 14A?
The writer was happy to change seats at first.
What had the old man been?

l.intro: A traveller tells a colleague about a difficult journey.

script.t: Kate, you look exhausted. Didn't you sleep on the plane?
Not a minute. We'd been waiting at the gate for three hours when they finally let us board.
Why the delay?
The cabin crew hadn't arrived. Then, just as we were taking off, a storm started.
Was there turbulence?
It was so bad that the drinks flew off the trays. The man in the aisle seat was praying.
And when you landed?
My suitcase had been sent to another city. I'd been standing at baggage reclaim for an hour before they told me.
It was such a terrible trip that you deserve a day off.
Tell that to my jet lag.

ex.q: How long did the passengers wait at the gate?
Why was the flight delayed?
Kate's suitcase arrived with her.
How does Kate feel now?

lessons.title: Narrative tenses, past perfect continuous; so / such…that
Listening: The worst flight of my life

3B.title: A really good ending?
words: An unexpected change at the end of a story
An ending that leaves you in suspense
The events that happen in a story
A book about a real person’s life
In the end, after a long time
In the main and most important way
Finally, after a series of events

g.title: The position of adverbs and adverbial phrases
g.rule:
Where an adverb goes depends on its type.

manner, place, time: usually at the endShe read the story quickly. · We met at the library last week.
frequency and degree: before the main verb, after beI hardly ever finish a novel. · It is incredibly short.
comment adverbs: at the beginningUnfortunately, the ending was predictable.

ex.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I read always the last page first.
I always read the last page first.
Always I read the last page first.

ex.q: ___, nobody knew how the story would end.
He speaks English very ___ (good).

talk: Tell the plot of a short story, film or series in two minutes. Do you like the ending?
Do you ever read the last page of a book first? Why or why not?

r.text:
How short can a story be? According to a famous legend, a writer once won a bet by producing one in six words. Whether or not it really happened, the idea has never gone away.

Today thousands of people regularly publish six-word stories online. Some are funny. Others are quietly devastating. The best ones usually end with a twist that makes you read them again immediately.

Teachers have enthusiastically adopted the form. Students who rarely finish a page will happily write ten tiny stories in a lesson. They quickly discover that every word has to work hard, and that an adverb in the wrong place ruins the rhythm completely.

Unfortunately, brevity is not easy. Most first attempts are just sentences. A real story, even a tiny one, needs a character, a change and, ideally, something left unsaid.

Here is mine: "Finally learned her language. She'd left."

ex.q: How long is the story in the legend?
What do the best six-word stories usually have?
Teachers have refused to use the form.
What does a real story need?
o: A character, a change and something unsaid

l.intro: Two friends talk about a novel they are both reading.

script.t: Luke, have you finished the book yet?
Nearly. Apparently there's a twist in the last chapter.
Don't tell me! I've only just started it.
I won't. Basically, the plot moves very slowly at first.
I noticed. I almost gave up after fifty pages.
Gradually it gets better. Eventually you can't put it down.
Ideally, I'd read it in one weekend.
Then stay off the internet. People carelessly post the ending everywhere.
Honestly, I prefer a predictable story to a ruined one.
You'll never guess this one. Every chapter ends on a cliffhanger.

ex.q: Dina has almost finished the book.
How does the plot move at first?
What advice does Luke give?
How does every chapter end?

lessons.title: The position of adverbs and adverbial phrases
Listening: Don't tell me the ending

4A.title: Stormy weather
words: A long period with little or no rain
A snowstorm with very strong winds
A period of unusually hot weather
Pollution in city air that makes it hard to see
Small balls of ice that fall like rain
Warm and wet, but not raining
When everything is covered with water
A violent storm with very strong winds
A flash of very bright light in the sky
Energy that will not run out, e.g. solar

g.title: Future perfect and future continuous
g.rule:
Look at the future from a point in the future.

finished before a future time → will have + past participleBy 2050, sea levels will have risen.
in progress at a future time → will be + -ingThis time next week I'll be skiing.
time expressionsby Friday · by the time you arrive · in ten years' time

ex.q: By the end of this year, I ___ my degree.
Don't call at eight. We ___ dinner.
In twenty years' time, most cars ___ (be) electric.

talk: What will you be doing this time next year? What will you have done by then?
How do you think the climate will have changed your region by 2050?

r.text:
Dear grandchildren,

By the time you read this, I will have been dead for some years, and you will be living in a world I can only imagine.

I expect that the summers will have become longer. Perhaps you will be spending July in the north, as people in my day went south. I hope the droughts will not have destroyed the orchards I planted.

Will people still be burning fossil fuels? I would like to think that by 2060 the last coal station will have closed, and that children will be learning about smog in history lessons.

We were not stupid, you know. We simply believed that somebody else would be solving the problem next year.

This afternoon it is drizzling, the garden is humid, and I will be planting one more tree before dinner. By the time it is tall, I will have gone. I hope you will be sitting under it.

With love,
Your grandfather

ex.q: Who is the letter written to?
What does the writer hope will have closed by 2060?
The writer says his generation was stupid.
What will he be doing before dinner?

l.intro: A radio presenter interviews a climate scientist.

script.t: Dr Ospanova, what will our summers be like in thirty years?
By 2050, average temperatures will have risen by about two degrees.
And what will that mean day to day?
We'll be having longer heatwaves, and farmers will be facing regular droughts.
Will winters disappear?
No, but blizzards will be rarer. Instead, it'll be pouring with rain more often.
Will we have stopped using fossil fuels by then?
I hope we will have replaced most of them. Otherwise smog will be getting worse in the cities.
Are you optimistic?
Cautiously. In ten years' time most new cars will be eco-friendly.

ex.q: By how much will temperatures have risen by 2050?
What will farmers be facing?
The scientist says blizzards will be more common.
How does she describe herself?

4B.title: A risky business
words: A person who likes doing dangerous or exciting things
The excited feeling in your body when you’re scared
Jumping from a plane with a parachute
Jumping from a bridge on an elastic rope
Insurance you buy before a trip
To look or behave like an older family member
To look after someone or something
Flying through the air in a special suit
Brave enough to do dangerous things

g.title: Zero and first conditionals, future time clauses
g.rule:
Use these for real situations.

always true → zero: if + present, presentIf you heat ice, it melts.
possible future → first: if + present, will / may / can / imperativeIf you don't wear a helmet, you'll get hurt.
time clauses + present, not willI'll text you as soon as I land. · Wait until it has stopped.
in caseTake a jacket in case it gets cold.

ex.q: I'll tell you as soon as I ___ any news.
Take your phone ___ you get lost.
You won't improve unless you ___ (practise).

talk: Are you a risk-taker? Talk about a risk you took and one you would never take.
What safety advice would you give a tourist visiting your country?

r.text:
Ask people what frightens them and they will mention sharks, plane crashes and bungee jumping. Ask an insurance company what actually kills us, and the list is far less dramatic: cars, stairs and sofas.

Psychologists explain it like this. If a danger is rare and spectacular, we remember it. If it is common and boring, we ignore it. Unless something appears on the news, we assume it will not happen to us.

This has practical consequences. People will pay for travel insurance when they go skydiving, but they will not wear a helmet on a bicycle unless the law makes them.

The real risk-takers, it turns out, are not the people who jump out of planes. They check their equipment twice. They are the ones who text while driving, and who will see the doctor "as soon as work calms down".

If you want an adrenaline rush, take up climbing. If you want to live longer, take the stairs carefully.

ex.q: What actually causes most deaths, according to insurers?
Why do we ignore common dangers?
People who jump out of planes are the most careless.
Who are the real risk-takers?

l.intro: An instructor prepares a nervous customer for a bungee jump.

script.t: Right. If you listen carefully, nothing will go wrong.
What happens if the rope breaks?
It doesn't. If a rope is used two hundred times, we replace it.
Should I close my eyes?
If you close them, you'll miss the best part. Take your time.
I'm not really a risk-taker. I take after my mother.
Don't jump until I say so. As soon as you hear three, lean forward.
Have you got my travel insurance details in case something happens?
Yes. Unless you tell me to stop, I'll start counting.
OK. If I survive, I'll take up something quieter. Like chess.

ex.q: When is a rope replaced?
The instructor tells him to close his eyes.
When should he lean forward?
What will he take up if he survives?

lessons.title: Zero and first conditionals, future time clauses
Reading: The risk we don't see

5A.title: I’m a survivor
words: A large mass of snow falling down a mountain
A simple structure that protects you from bad weather
A person who enters a building illegally
Sad because you are away from home
Happy because a worry or problem has gone
So surprised you cannot move or react
With little hope and ready to do anything
Feeling such strong emotions you do not know how to react
Bored or annoyed with something that has continued too long
Upset because someone was rude or ignored you
Continuing to live in a dangerous situation

g.title: Unreal conditionals
g.rule:
Use these to imagine a different present or past.

second: if + past, would + verbIf I were lost in a forest, I'd follow a river.
third: if + past perfect, would have + past participleIf they had taken a map, they wouldn't have got lost.
mixedIf I had listened, I wouldn't be here now.

ex.q: If I ___ what to do, I would have helped.
If we had more water, we ___ so worried.
If she hadn't called for help, she ___ (not / survive).

talk: How would you cope if you were lost somewhere wild for three days?
Tell a survival story you have read or seen. What would you have done?

r.text:
In February a 58-year-old teacher went cross-country skiing alone. She told nobody where she was going, and she left her phone in the car.

An avalanche blocked the path behind her. If she had turned back ten minutes earlier, she would have reached the road. Instead she spent three nights in a shelter she dug in the snow.

Rescuers say she did almost everything right. If she had kept walking, she would have become exhausted and lost. If she hadn't had a thermos and chocolate in her rucksack, she would probably not have survived the first night.

She is less proud of herself. "If I were a sensible person, I'd have told my husband my route," she says. "If I had taken the phone, they would have found me in an hour."

Would she ski alone again? "If anyone asked me today, I'd say no. Ask me again in spring."

ex.q: What mistake did the teacher make before she left?
How long was she in the snow?
Rescuers think she did almost everything wrong.
What helped her survive the first night?

l.intro: Two colleagues discuss a survival story in the news.

script.t: Did you read about the skier who survived the avalanche?
Yes. If he hadn't built a shelter, he would have frozen.
I'd have panicked. If I were buried in snow, I wouldn't know what to do.
Apparently he stayed calm. If he had tried to walk, he'd have got lost.
His family must have been desperate.
They were stunned when he phoned. If his battery had died, nobody would have found him.
Would you go skiing there now?
Only if I had a guide. I'd be homesick after one night alone.
If I'd been him, I'd never ski again.
He says he's going back next winter.

ex.q: How did the skier survive?
He tried to walk out and got lost.
How did his family feel when he phoned?
What is he going to do next winter?

lessons.title: Reading: Three days in the snow
Listening: What would you have done?

5B.title: Wish you were here
words: A feeling of sadness about something you did or did not do
Annoyed because you cannot do or change something
Making you feel silly in front of others
Making you want to do something great
Sad because something was not as good as you hoped
Rude in a way that upsets people
The quality of telling the truth
Showing a lot of interest and excitement
When someone says no to you or does not accept you

g.title: wish for present / future; wish for past regrets
g.rule:
After wish, go one tense back from the real situation.

present → wish + pastI wish I had more time. · I wish I could drive.
annoying habits → wish + wouldI wish you wouldn't interrupt.
past regrets → wish + past perfectI wish I had studied harder.
If only = strongerIf only I hadn't said that.

ex.q: I wish I ___ so much last night.
I wish my neighbours ___ so much noise.
If only I ___ (can) speak three languages.

talk: What do you regret doing or not doing? What do you wish were different now?
What habits of other people annoy you? I wish people wouldn't…

r.text:
A nurse who spent years caring for the elderly once kept a record of what her patients told her. Almost nobody said they wished they had worked harder.

The commonest regret was simple. People wished they had spent more time with friends. "If only I had picked up the phone," one man said. Many wished they had been brave enough to say what they really felt.

Younger people, interviewed for comparison, had different wishes. They wished they earned more, that their flat were bigger, that their boss wouldn't email them on Sundays. Their wishes were about the present, and mostly about things.

The nurse draws a gentle conclusion. "The old don't say 'I wish I'd had a better car'. They say 'I wish I'd gone to that wedding'."

It is an exhausting thought, and an inspiring one. Is there somebody you wish you had called this week? There is still time.

ex.q: Who kept a record of patients' regrets?
What was the commonest regret?
o: Not spending more time with friends

ex.q: Younger people's wishes were mostly about the past.
What do the old wish, according to the nurse?
o: That they had gone to the wedding
That they had a better car

l.intro: Two friends talk about regrets.

script.t: Chris, do you have any regrets?
Plenty. I wish I'd learned to play an instrument as a child.
It's not too late. I wish I had more free time, though.
I wish my boss wouldn't email me at midnight. It's infuriating.
Mine does too. If only I hadn't accepted that promotion.
Really? I thought you found it inspiring.
At first. Now it's just exhausting. I wish I could go back to my old team.
I wish I'd travelled before I started working.
If only we were twenty again.
Honestly? I wouldn't change much. I just wish I worried less.

ex.q: What does Chris wish he had learned?
What annoys Chris about his boss?
Madina is happy she accepted the promotion.
What does Madina wish in the end?

lessons.title: wish for present / future; wish for past regrets
Listening: I wish I hadn't said that

talk: How have your sleeping habits changed since you were a child?
Describe something new you had to get used to. How long did it take?

r.text:
When I moved to southern Spain, the first thing I had to get used to was the silence at three in the afternoon. Shops were shut. Streets were empty. I used to think the siesta was a myth for tourists. It is not.

At home I used to eat lunch at my desk in ten minutes. Here, lunch takes an hour and a half, and afterwards many people lie down. At first I couldn't get used to sleeping in daylight. I lay on the bed feeling guilty.

Now, two years later, I'm used to it. I'm also used to having dinner at ten and going to bed after midnight, which once seemed insane.

Researchers are divided about whether a nap is good for you. A short one seems to help memory; a long one can cause insomnia.

My mother visited last month. "You didn't use to be so relaxed," she said, yawning. By day three she was napping too.

ex.q: What surprised the writer first?
o: The silence at three in the afternoon

ex.q: How long does lunch take in Spain?
The writer still can't sleep in daylight.
What do researchers say about naps?
o: A short one may help memory

l.intro: A nurse talks about working night shifts.

script.t: How long have you been working nights?
Two years. I used to sleep eight hours without a problem.
And now?
I'm used to sleeping during the day, but it took months.
What was hardest to get used to?
Eating dinner at three in the morning. I still can't get used to that.
Do you ever oversleep?
I used to, so now I have three alarms. And I take a short nap before work.
Would you go back to days?
I'm so used to the quiet that I'd probably miss it. I don't even yawn any more.

ex.q: How long has the nurse worked nights?
She found it easy to get used to sleeping during the day.
What can't she get used to?

g.rule:

talk: What music do you remember loving as a child? What do you tend to listen to now?
Does music change your mood? Give examples.

r.text:
You are brushing your teeth, and suddenly you notice that you have been humming the same four bars for an hour. Psychologists have a name for it: an earworm.

Almost everybody gets them. They tend to be songs with a simple melody and one unexpected jump, and they usually arrive when the mind is not busy. People often remember hearing the song in a shop that morning without having paid attention.

Trying to forget the tune rarely works. In fact, the more you try to stop thinking about it, the longer it stays. Researchers suggest listening to the whole song once, because the brain seems to want to finish it. Others recommend chewing gum, or learning to hum something else.

Musicians, interestingly, suffer more than the rest of us. A cellist in one study couldn't stop hearing a concerto she had failed to play well at sixteen.

It could be worse. Most people say they enjoy their earworms. They only regret choosing them so badly.

ex.q: What is an earworm?
o: A song stuck in your head

ex.q: When do earworms usually arrive?
o: When the mind is not busy

ex.q: Trying hard to forget the tune usually works.
What do researchers suggest?
o: Listening to the whole song once

l.intro: Two parents talk after a concert.

Yes, but he kept stopping to check the music.
The choir was excellent. Do you remember singing in one at school?
I do. I tried to learn the saxophone too, but I gave up practising.
You should try taking lessons again.
I can't afford to buy a saxophone. Maybe I'll stop making excuses, though.
The orchestra needs adults. Remember to ask the conductor.

talk: Describe an argument you had or saw. What should the people have done differently?

r.text:
It started with a spoon. My brother had put a wet spoon back in the sugar. By the end of the evening we were arguing about a holiday in 2014.

A family therapist I later interviewed was not surprised. "The spoon can't have been the real problem," she said. "Somebody must have been feeling ignored for weeks."

She hears the same story every day. One partner should have said something months ago and didn't. The other might have noticed and chose not to. When the argument finally comes, it attaches itself to the first small thing available.

Her advice is practical. You shouldn't say "you always" or "you never". You should describe one event, and what you would rather happen next time.

I tried it. I told my brother that I'd rather he dried the spoon. He looked at me as if I had lost my mind. Then he said he would rather I didn't leave my shoes in the hall. We must have talked for two hours.

ex.q: What started the argument?
o: A wet spoon in the sugar

ex.q: What does the therapist think the real problem was?
The therapist recommends saying 'you always'.

o: That the writer didn't leave shoes in the hall

My laptop is here. The wind might have pushed it open.
You should have told the landlord about that lock.
I did! He should have fixed it weeks ago.
I'd rather not argue. Let's call him now.
I'd rather you called him. He never denies anything to you.

talk: Can you tell what a person is feeling from their body language? Give examples.
Describe an actor's performance that impressed you.

r.text:
Professional card players spend years learning to control their faces. What they cannot easily control is everything else.

A former champion describes what she looks for. A player whose hands look relaxed but whose ankle is moving under the table is usually nervous. Someone who suddenly sounds cheerful may be hiding a weak hand. A person who stares at you for too long looks as if they are trying to seem confident.

Actors use the same knowledge in reverse. To seem angry, it is not enough to frown. The shoulders rise, the breathing changes and the voice sounds tighter. If the body disagrees with the face, the audience feels that something is wrong, even if they can't say what.

Can ordinary people learn to read these signals? A little. But the champion offers a warning. "A shrug can mean ten things. It feels like mind-reading, and it looks like science. Mostly, it's a good guess."

ex.q: What can card players not easily control?

o: Reading body language is mostly a good guess

l.intro: An acting teacher gives feedback to a student.

script.t: That was better, but you still look as if you're reading the lines.
It feels natural to me.
It sounds flat. When you say sorry, you should look as though you mean it.
How? Should I frown?
Try a small shrug first. Then look at her. Don't stare.
Like this?
Yes. Now you look like a real person. Your voice sounds warmer too.
It feels strange to wave at nobody.
It looks right from here. And don't scratch your wrist. You seem nervous.
I am nervous. Does it look that obvious?

talk: What can people do to protect their homes and phones from crime?

r.text:
Five years ago, bicycle theft was the commonest crime in a small Dutch-style university town. Hundreds were stolen every month, and almost none were recovered. Students had their bikes taken so often that many stopped buying them.

Then the council tried something unusual. A thousand yellow bicycles were bought, and they were left unlocked around the town. Anyone could take one. It was hoped that nobody would steal what was already free.

At first the scheme was laughed at. Within a month, two hundred bikes had been thrown in the river or sold. The council is said to have considered giving up.

Instead, each bike was fitted with a cheap tracker, and local teenagers were paid to repair them. Vandalism fell. Thefts of private bikes are reported to have dropped by half, although nobody is sure why.

The mayor has a theory. "A crime is easier to commit against a stranger," he says. "These bikes belong to everybody. They have been adopted."

ex.q: What was the commonest crime in the town?

o: Left a thousand free bikes around the town

ex.q: The scheme was an immediate success.

o: A crime is easier against a stranger

l.intro: A newsreader and a reporter cover a crime story.

Thank you. The painting is believed to have been taken at about three this morning.

Yes, staff are being questioned as we speak. The alarm is said to have been repaired only last week.

It is estimated to be worth two million. The gallery had its security checked in May.

talk: How do you decide whether a news story is true?
Tell a news story you heard recently. Who said, claimed or denied what?

r.text:
On a Tuesday in spring, a website reported that a well-known bakery chain was closing all its shops. By evening the story had been shared two hundred thousand times. It was not true.

A journalist decided to trace it backwards. The website admitted copying it from a blog. The blogger denied inventing it and blamed a post she had seen. The author of the post apologised for causing confusion: he had been joking, and he insisted on having written "April Fool" at the end, which somebody had cut.

The bakery asked the website to remove the article. The editor refused to do so for six hours and then agreed to publish a correction. It was shared four thousand times.

That is the uncomfortable lesson. A sensational headline persuades people to click. A correction reminds nobody of anything.

The journalist now advises her readers to do one thing before sharing: wait ten minutes. Most false stories, she says, don't survive ten minutes of thought.

ex.q: What did the website report?
Where did the story really start?
o: As a joke in a post

ex.q: The correction was shared more often than the false story.
What does the journalist advise?

l.intro: A journalism teacher talks to a student about a story.

script.t: Zhanna, where did this headline come from?

No, but a colleague advised me not to trust the source.
Good advice. I'd recommend calling the mayor's office yourself.

Then remind them that we want to be objective. A biased story helps nobody.
I'll try again. I promised to finish it by Friday.

r.text:
Advertising has a reputation for exaggeration. So when a small shoe company launched a campaign that listed the faults of its own product, the industry laughed.

The posters said that the shoes were not waterproof, that they took a week to feel comfortable, and that they cost more than they should. In spite of this, or because of it, sales doubled.

Why? Consumers have heard every promise. Although most slogans are ignored, an admission is surprising, and people stop to read it. The company had also designed the campaign so that every criticism was followed by a quiet strength: despite being expensive, the shoes could be repaired for free.

Bigger brands tried to copy the idea in order to seem equally sincere. It rarely worked. Honesty that has clearly been produced by a marketing department is still marketing.

The founder is relaxed about it. "We told the truth so as not to disappoint anyone," she says. "Even though it was good business, that wasn't the reason."

script.t: Ben, we need a new slogan so that people remember the brand.

We could offer a free sample so as not to look too pushy.
As long as the advert isn't misleading.
It won't be. I wrote everything down so that the lawyers could check it.
Then let's expand the team for the launch.
Though not before we see the first sales.

talk: Compare two cities you know: transport, housing, noise, things to do.

r.text:
Thirty years ago it was a fishing town with one traffic light. Today it is a megacity of nine million, and the traffic is legendary.

Newcomers are surprised by how much has been done. Public transport is modern, the airport is efficient, and there is more green space than you would expect. The research carried out by the university suggests that air quality has actually improved.

The problems are less visible. Housing is the main one. Accommodation in the centre is unaffordable, so workers live on the sprawling outskirts and spend three hours a day travelling. The police are well funded, but the suburbs have little evidence of their presence.

Then there is the question of identity. The city is proudly multicultural, and most children are bilingual. Yet older residents say that the neighbourhood spirit has gone. "We had no money and plenty of time," one tells me. "Now the furniture is better and nobody visits."

The news is not all bad. Progress rarely is.

g.rule:

talk: Which scientific discovery do you think is the most important? Why?

r.text:
Every generation of scientists has believed things that the next generation found ridiculous.

For centuries, all educated people were sure that the Earth stood still. Every doctor recommended removing blood from patients, and most of them thought fresh air was dangerous. Neither idea survived proper experiments.

In the twentieth century, both sugar and fat were blamed for heart disease at different times, and no theory lasted more than a few decades. Any student who had suggested that stomach problems were caused by bacteria would have been laughed at. Two researchers proved it, one of them by drinking the bacteria himself.

None of this means that science is unreliable. All of these errors were corrected by scientists, not by their critics. Each discovery replaced a weaker explanation with a stronger one.

It does suggest some modesty. Most of what we know is probably right. A few things are certainly wrong, and either we shall find out which, or our grandchildren will.

Either a headache or nothing at all. All of them recover in an hour.
I'd volunteer, as long as I'm not a guinea pig for long.

talk: Who is the best public speaker you have heard? What makes them good?

r.text:
At the end of the school year, one student is chosen to give a speech to the whole school. This year it was Dinara, who had never spoken in public and who describes herself as the quietest girl in the class.

She prepared for a month. A teacher gave her three pieces of advice. First, find a face in the audience and speak to it. Second, don't learn the speech by heart; learn the order of the ideas. Third, the first sentence matters more than the rest.

On the day, the microphone failed. The headmaster offered to postpone. Dinara walked to the front of the stage and spoke without it.

She talked about the history of her grandmother's village, and about the day the school there closed. She did not use a single note. By and large, people remember the silence in the hall more than the applause.

Afterwards somebody asked whether she had been afraid. "Sick with fear," she said. "That's why I looked at my grandmother."

ex.q: What went wrong on the day?

l.intro: A coach helps a student prepare a short speech.

Good. Give an example from the UK or Kazakhstan, not from space.

By and large, a short story works better than a joke.
I'm sick and tired of being afraid. Let's practise.
